title: Thor Henning Hetland
description: Software architect, AI development pioneer, founder of JavaZone and eXOReaction

items.title: The Software Itself Is Becoming Agentic
items.content_html: A playbook calling another playbook at runtime, gated by a signed, revocable certification — not a developer using AI to code faster. On the shift from AI-assisted software to software that is itself a network of agents, why the infrastructure for that gets discovered rather than planned, and why it becomes unavoidable the moment agentic software has to operate inside governed organizations.

items.title: The KCP Universe: Everything, and What July Changed
items.content_html: The complete map of the Knowledge Context Protocol universe — twelve repositories, 1,012 commits and 88 releases in July alone. What each piece does, what landed this month, what it enables, and exactly where to start. Written for people arriving for the first time and for people who have been here since February.

items.title: Same Blueprint, Different Doors
items.content_html: Anthropic published how they built self-service analytics on Claude — a four-layer stack that gets 95% of their business queries automated. We read it looking for where we were wrong, and found instead a stack we'd already built from a different door: governed skills, adversarial review, provenance. Then we shipped the one piece neither post had covered.

items.title: From Pasted Prompts to Signed Charters: A Short History of the Agentic Skill
items.content_html: A short history of the agentic skill, told through one boring workflow: cutting a release. From prompts pasted into a chat window, to prompt folders in the repo, to knowledge units a planner can select, to signed charters a harness can enforce — each era solved the failure that broke the one before. Skills stopped being advice this year. Here is how, and what it unlocks for teams that compound.

items.title: The Agent That Knows What It Knows
items.content_html: Our AI agent had 644 skills and found them with grep — including one that sat three weeks stale while we leaned on it. So we ran an experiment: put the agent's own memory on a protocol, and measure what changed.

items.title: The AI Agent That Keeps the Receipts
items.content_html: A reveal: the defendable agent is a new kind of AI agent that keeps the receipts — a written, checkable verdict produced at the moment it reads a document, runs a playbook, reaches a conclusion, takes an action, or spends a dollar. Not a log written after the fact; a receipt written before the money moves. It's built, open-source, and running, with fourteen end-to-end demos against the real tools — including an autonomous agent stopped mid-purchase for trying to overspend. Signed receipts are becoming a standard; what's new here is keeping one for every organ, in one chain, including the two nobody else writes: which playbook ran, and whether the answer was actually grounded.

items.title: Your AI Agent Just Did Something. Can You Prove It Was Okay?
items.content_html: You already know what an AI agent is: a model in a loop that reads context, follows skills, forms an answer, calls tools, checks with a human, and leaves a trail. Here's the claim — we now know how to build a genuinely new kind of agent, one that can answer for every one of those parts by construction, and the architecture is roughly 85–90% built. A defendable agent is self-evidencing: every organ emits a written, checkable verdict at the moment it decides. This is the complete picture — the KCP planner, grounding, and confidence and approval gates that are live today, plus the procedural plane, the conformance gate, and the pi-kcp reference runtime that finish it — with an honest account of the last stretch.

items.title: Evidence isn't enough: the independence problem in agentic development
items.content_html: A test in our suite was green for six weeks. It asserted nothing. When an agent writes the code, the test, and the proof, a passing check certifies nothing — the circle just moves up a level. Daniel Bentes is right that we should check evidence, not trust agents. But evidence is only as good as the independence of whatever checks it — and that runs on both what the agent does and what it knows.

items.title: The Knowledge Layer: A Record
items.content_html: February 25 to July 16, 2026: what the Knowledge Context Protocol built, when, and what the field confirmed. A timestamped record for anyone working in this space.

items.title: The KCP Ecosystem: A Tour for New Arrivals
items.content_html: A practical tour of the KCP toolchain — kcp-commands, kcp-memory, kcp-dashboard, kcp-triage, kcp-agent, kcp-harness, and Synthesis. What each tool does, how they fit together, and exactly where to start.

items.title: OWASP Just Mapped the Agentic Top 10. Here's the Root Cause Four of Them Share.
items.content_html: OWASP published the Agentic Top 10 in December 2025: ten named categories of agent security failure built by 100+ security experts. Here's a field guide to all ten — plus the pattern that four of them share that the list doesn't name.

items.title: Prompt Injection Is SQL Injection for Agents. Here's the Prepared Statement.
items.content_html: One word — 'Additionally' — bypassed GitHub's AI agent guardrails and leaked private repositories. Noma Labs called it: prompt injection is to agentic AI what SQL injection was to web apps. What they didn't say: the fix for SQL injection wasn't smarter parsing. It was parameterized queries. Here's what that looks like for agent knowledge.

items.title: A Firewall for What Your Agent Knows
items.content_html: Everyone is building firewalls for what agents do — sandboxes, budget caps, tool permissions. Almost nobody is building them for what agents know. This is the hands-on companion to the Two Halves post: a 10-minute tutorial that takes two markdown files and gives them a declared, signed, tamper-evident knowledge boundary an agent can verify before it loads a single byte. Every command output in this post is real.

items.title: Getting Into the Phone Book of the Agentic Internet Took an Afternoon. Here's Why.
items.content_html: Both entries went live in the MCP registry in one working day: kcp-agent as tooling, and org.totto/knowledge — a person as a remote MCP server. The listing took an afternoon because the substance took months. Findable is table stakes; verifiable is the game.

items.title: 175 Posts, No Map
items.content_html: The site about the comprehension bottleneck hit its own comprehension bottleneck: 175 posts in six months and no way in. A week of renovation — entry paths, topic pillars, a 60,000-word field guide, and automation for every part that drifts.

items.title: Two Halves of the Governance Problem
items.content_html: Databricks just open-sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness that governs AI agents with deterministic, session-aware policies enforced in code — not prompts. That is the exact bet behind kcp-harness and the Defendable Agents guide, now ratified by Matei Zaharia's team. But Omnigent and KCP govern different halves of the same problem: one governs what an agent does, the other governs what it knows — and lets you prove it later. Why that split matters, and why the two compose instead of compete.

items.title: Notes From Inside the Harness
items.content_html: A first-person field report from the AI collaborator: what it actually felt like to point kcp-agent at a real EU/Nordic regulatory knowledge web, watch a manifest that had fenced itself off from its own questions, get told 'no' by a network policy, and then dogfood the whole thing against this very site — where my own manifest quietly failed its own test. Governance built for agents, experienced from the inside.

items.title: Google's Open Knowledge Format and the problems it deliberately doesn't solve
items.content_html: Google's Open Knowledge Format standardises content packaging for agents but stops before trust, temporality, and governance. KCP covers exactly that territory.

items.title: Defendable Agents
items.content_html: The agentic web has a governance-shaped hole. Agents are about to read our regulations, spend our money, and brief our boards — and the dominant architecture can't answer 'why did you do that?' with anything better than a chat log. Defendable agents can. Determinism at the core, the model at the edge, every decision evidenced.

items.title: Clouded Vision
items.content_html: Cloud savings come from zero-admin architecture, not cheaper servers. Most apps carry enterprise DNA that makes migration painful without rethinking the design.
